cards.q: A laptop can have a 1TB hard-disk drive (HDD) or a 512GB solid-state drive (SSD). If cost and capacity were not issues, why might you opt for the SSD?
cards.right: No moving parts, so faster and more durable
wrong: Stores data magnetically, so it is faster
Non-volatile, but an HDD loses data when off
Spinning platters reach data more quickly
cards.why: An SSD is flash memory with no moving parts: no head has to move to the data, so it reads and writes faster, and nothing mechanical can break if the laptop is knocked.
cards.hook: SSD = Silent, Solid, Speedy: no spinning disk, no moving head.

cards.q: Apart from speed, which of these is a reason to choose an SSD over an HDD in a laptop?
cards.right: Uses less power, so the battery lasts longer
wrong: Its read/write head is safer when knocked about
It keeps data in RAM, so nothing is ever lost
It costs less per gigabyte than an HDD does
cards.why: An SSD is completely electronic, so it consumes less power (and is quieter, lighter and safe from magnets). It has no read/write head at all, and it costs more per GB.
cards.hook: No motor to spin: less power, less noise, less weight.

cards.q: The program counter is a special register in the processor. What is its purpose?
cards.right: Holds the address of the next instruction
wrong: Holds the next instruction to be executed
Holds the address of the data being fetched
Counts how many programs are running
cards.why: The PC contains the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed. The instruction itself goes into the CIR; the address of the data goes in the MAR.
cards.hook: The PC points to WHERE the next instruction is, never the instruction itself.
keys: memory address of the next instruction

cards.q: In the fetch stage, the address in the program counter is copied to another register. What happens to the program counter straight after the fetch?
cards.right: It is incremented to point at the next one
wrong: It is cleared to 0 until the next fetch
It is loaded with the fetched instruction
It is decremented back to the last one
cards.why: The PC's address is copied to the MAR, the instruction is fetched, and the PC is incremented so it points to the following instruction (unless a jump changes it).
cards.hook: Fetch, then PC + 1: it is always one step ahead.

cards.q: The World Wide Web lets web pages, voice and streams travel seamlessly because of the protocols it uses. What is meant by a protocol?
cards.right: An agreed set of rules for devices to communicate
wrong: A unique address given to each device
A program that requests and displays web pages
A device that forwards packets between networks
cards.why: A protocol is a set of rules and procedures for network communication: an agreed way for two computers, devices or processes to format, send and receive data.
cards.hook: Protocol = the rules of the conversation that both sides agree on first.
keys: rules and procedures for network communication

cards.q: A browser requests a web page (an HTML document) from a web server, and the page is sent back with an added encryption layer. Which protocol is this?
cards.right: HTTPS
wrong: HTTP
FTP
SMTP
cards.why: HTTP exchanges WWW documents (typically HTML) between server and browser; HTTPS is HTTP plus an added security layer that encrypts and decrypts the data.
cards.hook: The S in HTTPS is for Secure: the same pages, encrypted.
keys: HTTP plus an added security layer

cards.q: Which protocol breaks a message into packets, hands them to IP, and reassembles them in the right order at the destination?
cards.right: TCP
wrong: IP
UDP
DNS
cards.why: TCP splits messages into numbered packets and reassembles and orders them at the destination. IP only routes each packet; UDP sends packets with no ordering or checking.
cards.hook: TCP Takes Care of Packets: splits, numbers, rebuilds. IP just delivers.

cards.q: What is the purpose of IP (Internet Protocol)?
cards.right: Routes packets from source to destination
wrong: Splits messages into packets and reorders them
Translates domain names into addresses
Exchanges HTML documents with a browser
cards.why: IP addresses each packet and routes it from the source to the destination across connected networks. Splitting and reordering is TCP's job; translating names is DNS's.
cards.hook: IP is the postal address on each packet: it gets it there, nothing more.
keys: routes it from the source to the destination

cards.q: A half-adder has inputs A and B. Output C comes from an AND gate on A and B. What is the value of C when A and B are both 0?
wrong: Undefined: no input is 1
Equal to S
cards.why: C = A AND B = 0 AND 0 = 0. An AND gate outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1.
cards.hook: AND is strict: both must be 1. C is the carry, 1 only for 1 + 1.

cards.q: In a half-adder, the carry C = A AND B. For which inputs is C = 1?
cards.right: Only when A = 1 and B = 1
wrong: When A and B are different
When A or B (or both) is 1
Only when A = 0 and B = 0
cards.why: AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1, so C = 1 only for A = 1, B = 1: in binary 1 + 1 = 10, which carries a 1.
cards.hook: Carry only happens for 1 + 1 = 10.

cards.q: Half-adder: C = A AND B, and S = (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B). What are S and C when A and B are both 1?
cards.why: NOT A = 0 and NOT B = 0, so both AND gates feeding S give 0, and S = 0 OR 0 = 0. C = 1 AND 1 = 1. As binary: 1 + 1 = 10.
cards.hook: Write the value on every wire, gate by gate. 1 + 1 = 10: sum 0, carry 1.

cards.q: In a half-adder, S = (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B). Which single gate gives the same output S?
cards.right: XOR
wrong: OR
XNOR
NAND
cards.why: S is 1 only when exactly one input is 1 (A and B differ), which is XOR. OR would also give 1 for 1, 1; XNOR is 1 when they match.
cards.hook: XOR = eXclusive OR: one or the other, not both.

cards.q: Why is data stored in computers in binary format?
cards.right: Transistors are switches with two states, on/off
wrong: Binary numbers take up less memory than denary
Each transistor can hold any one digit from 0 to 9
Binary is the only base that a CPU can add in
cards.why: A processor's circuits are made of transistors, switches set by signals of 0V or 5V. Binary's 1 and 0 match the on and off states of a transistor.
cards.hook: 1 = on (5V), 0 = off (0V): one switch, one bit.
keys: on and off states of a transistor

cards.q: A transistor carries either 5V or 0V. Why is using only these two states more reliable than using ten voltage levels for the digits 0–9?
cards.right: Two states are easy to tell apart despite noise
wrong: Ten levels would need more transistors
Two states let the CPU skip error checks
Binary numbers have fewer digits than denary
cards.why: With only two possible states a signal is read correctly even if the voltage wobbles a little, so binary is more reliable than any other number system.
cards.hook: Two states: far apart, hard to confuse.
keys: more reliable than any other number system

cards.q: Which of these is a correct difference between RAM and ROM?
cards.right: RAM is volatile; ROM keeps its data with no power
wrong: ROM is volatile; RAM keeps its data with no power
RAM is read-only; ROM can be written to
ROM holds the programs in use; RAM the boot code
cards.why: RAM is volatile and loses its contents when switched off; ROM is non-volatile. RAM can be written to, ROM is read-only. ROM is used in start-up, RAM in normal operation.
cards.hook: ROM = Read-Only Memory: it Remembers On power-off.

cards.q: A computer's start-up (boot) instructions must survive when the power is off and must not be changed by accident. Which memory holds them?
cards.right: ROM, as it is non-volatile and read-only
wrong: RAM, as it is the fastest main memory
ROM, as it is volatile and reset each boot
RAM, as it can be written to at start-up
cards.why: ROM is non-volatile (keeps its contents without power) and read-only, so it holds the start-up instructions; RAM is used in normal operation after start-up.
cards.hook: Boot code lives in ROM: fixed and kept with the power off.

cards.q: Explain how increasing the amount of RAM on a computer might improve its performance.
cards.right: More fits in RAM, so less swapping to slow disk
wrong: More RAM raises the CPU's clock speed
RAM keeps programs after power-off: no reloading
More RAM gives more space for saving files
cards.why: More applications and data can be loaded in RAM at once, so the CPU spends less time loading from secondary storage (paging, thrashing) and programs respond faster.
cards.hook: Bigger desk, fewer trips to the filing cabinet (the disk).
keys: less time loading from secondary storage

cards.q: When RAM is full, the operating system moves parts of programs out to secondary storage and back again. What is this called?
cards.right: Paging
wrong: Caching
Spooling
Pipelining
cards.why: Paging swaps pages of memory between RAM and secondary storage (virtual memory). Too much of it is thrashing; more RAM means less paging and faster programs.
cards.hook: Pages go out to the disk when the RAM desk is full.

cards.q: Differentiate between HTTP and HTTPS.
cards.right: HTTPS encrypts the data (SSL/TLS); HTTP does not
wrong: HTTP encrypts the data; HTTPS sends plain text
HTTPS compresses pages so they load faster
HTTPS hides the IP address; HTTP shows it
cards.why: HTTP is unsecured; HTTPS is HTTP with a security layer (SSL/TLS) that encrypts data between browser and server, and it needs an SSL certificate signed by a CA.
cards.hook: The S is for Secure: same web pages, sent encrypted.
keys: encrypts data between browser and server

cards.q: Which port numbers do HTTP and HTTPS normally send data over?
cards.right: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443
wrong: HTTP 443, HTTPS 80
HTTP 80, HTTPS 8080
HTTP 21, HTTPS 22
cards.why: HTTP sends data over port 80 and HTTPS uses port 443. (21 is FTP, 22 is SSH, 8080 is an alternative HTTP port.)
cards.hook: 80 for plain, 443 for secure: the bigger number has the lock.

cards.q: TCP sends a message as packets. How does TCP make sure a packet lost on the way is not missing at the other end?
cards.right: No acknowledgement before a timeout, so it resends
wrong: IP finds the lost packet and reroutes it
The receiver rebuilds it from the other packets
Every packet is sent twice in case one is lost
cards.why: Reliability comes from acknowledgements and timeouts: if no acknowledgement arrives within the timeout, TCP resends the packet or the whole message.
cards.hook: TCP waits for a 'got it' (ACK); no ACK in time, send again.

cards.q: The packets of one message take different routes and arrive out of order. How does the receiving TCP put them back in the correct order?
cards.right: Using each packet's sequence number
wrong: Using each packet's IP address
Using the time each packet arrived
Using the MAC address of each router
cards.why: TCP breaks the message into packets, numbers each one, and passes them to IP. At the receiving end it reassembles them in the correct order using the sequence numbers.
cards.hook: Number the pages before you post them, then sort by number.

cards.q: What is an operating system?
cards.right: System software that controls the computer's hardware
wrong: The hardware that runs all the application software
An application, such as a browser or word processor
Firmware in ROM that only starts the computer up
cards.why: An OS is the software that controls the hardware of a computer; it is an interface between other software and the hardware, or the user and the machine.
cards.hook: The OS sits in the middle: user and apps above, hardware below.
keys: interface between other software and the hardware

cards.q: An operating system has four layers: I/O Management, File System, Memory Management and Processor Scheduling. Which one decides which job runs next and for how long?
cards.right: Processor Scheduling
wrong: Memory Management
I/O Management
File System
cards.why: Processor Scheduling decides which job runs next and for how long (first come first served, shortest job first, round robin), allowing multitasking.
cards.hook: The scheduler is the queue manager for the CPU.
keys: decides which job runs next and for how long

cards.q: Of the OS layers I/O Management, File System, Memory Management and Processor Scheduling, which allocates RAM and swaps data between secondary storage and RAM?
cards.right: Memory Management
wrong: File System
Processor Scheduling
I/O Management
cards.why: Memory Management allocates RAM, loads data from secondary to primary storage and swaps it back out. The File System tracks where files are on the disk.
cards.hook: Memory manager = RAM landlord: hands out space, takes it back.

cards.q: What is the function of the File System layer of an operating system?
cards.right: Tracks where files are and controls access to them
wrong: Allocates RAM to each program that is running
Reaches printers and screens through device drivers
Decides which job gets to use the CPU next
cards.why: The File System keeps track of where files are located (e.g. FAT), controls access to files and handles file security. Drivers are I/O Management; RAM is Memory Management.
cards.hook: File system = the library catalogue: where each file is, who may open it.
keys: keeps track of where files are located

cards.q: Rows (P, Q) are (False, False), (False, True), (True, False), (True, True). In that order, what is the column for `not P or not Q`?
cards.right: True, True, True, False
wrong: False, False, False, True
True, False, False, False
False, True, True, True
cards.why: not P is True, True, False, False and not Q is True, False, True, False. OR them: only the last row has both False, so True, True, True, False.
cards.hook: Fill not P and not Q first, then OR the two new columns.
keys: only the last row has both False

cards.q: An Eircode check uses `if ((not test_eircode[1].isdigit()) or (not test_eircode[2].isdigit())):`. With P and Q the two isdigit() tests, when is `not P or not Q` False?
cards.right: Only when both characters are digits
wrong: Only when neither character is a digit
When exactly one of them is a digit
Whenever the second character is a digit
cards.why: not P or not Q is False only when not P and not Q are both False, i.e. P = True and Q = True: characters 2 and 3 are both digits, so the code does not return False.
cards.hook: An OR is False only when every part is False.

cards.q: Rows (P, Q) are (False, False), (False, True), (True, False), (True, True). In that order, what is the column for `P and Q`?
cards.right: False, False, False, True
wrong: False, True, True, True
True, True, True, False
False, True, True, False
cards.why: P and Q is True only when both P and Q are True, which is the last row only: False, False, False, True.
cards.hook: AND needs both: one True row out of four.
keys: True only when both P and Q are True

cards.q: Rows (P, Q) are (False, False), (False, True), (True, False), (True, True). In that order, what is the column for `not (P and Q)`?
cards.right: True, True, True, False
wrong: True, False, False, False
False, False, False, True
False, True, True, False
cards.why: P and Q is False, False, False, True; not (P and Q) flips that column: True, True, True, False, the same as not P or not Q.
cards.hook: Work inside the brackets first, then flip the whole column.

cards.q: `not P or not Q` and `not (P and Q)` have the same truth table. P = test_eircode[1].isdigit(), Q = test_eircode[2].isdigit(). Which line has the same meaning as line 16?
cards.right: `if not (P and Q):`
wrong: `if not P and not Q:`
`if not (P or Q):`
`if (P and Q):`
cards.why: The truth tables match, so not P or not Q can be written not (P and Q): if not (test_eircode[1].isdigit() and test_eircode[2].isdigit()):
cards.hook: De Morgan: break the bracket, flip AND to OR (and back).

cards.q: Embedded systems are a combination of hardware and software. What is meant by hardware?
cards.right: The physical components of a computer system
wrong: The programs executed by the processor
The data stored on a computer's disk
Any device that connects to the Internet
cards.why: Hardware is the physical components of a computer system: processor, memory, storage devices, input and output devices, peripherals, registers, logic gates.
cards.hook: Hardware: if you can touch it (or kick it), it's hardware.
keys: physical components of a computer system

cards.q: What is meant by software?
cards.right: Programs (instructions) executed by the processor
wrong: The physical parts of a computer you can touch
The circuits that carry out the instructions
Only the operating system, not applications
cards.why: Software is the programs, the instructions, that are executed by the processor: any named application (Chrome, Word) or system software (Windows, Linux).
cards.hook: Software is the instructions; hardware is what follows them.
keys: instructions, that are executed by the processor

cards.q: Which pair gives one example of hardware and then one example of software, in that order?
cards.right: A keyboard, then Microsoft Windows
wrong: Microsoft Windows, then a keyboard
A processor, then RAM
Google Chrome, then Microsoft Word
cards.why: A keyboard is a physical input device (hardware); Windows is an operating system, a program the processor runs (software). RAM is hardware; Chrome and Word are both software.
cards.hook: Name real things: CPU, keyboard (hardware); Windows, Chrome (software).

cards.q: Embedded systems use sensors for digital or analogue inputs. Which of these is a digital sensor?
cards.right: A push-button switch
wrong: A temperature sensor
A light sensor
A humidity sensor
cards.why: A pushbutton, switch or keypad is digital: it is only ever on or off. Temperature, light and humidity are measured on a smooth scale, so their sensors are analogue.
cards.hook: Digital = a light switch (on/off). Analogue = a dimmer (any level).

cards.q: Which of these is an analogue sensor?
cards.right: A temperature sensor
wrong: A push button
A keypad
An on/off switch
cards.why: A temperature sensor measures a value that varies continuously over a range, so it is analogue. Buttons, keypads and switches give only on/off values: digital.
cards.hook: Analogue sensors read a scale; digital ones read yes or no.

cards.q: What is the difference between a digital input and an analogue input?
cards.right: Digital: two discrete values; analogue: any in a range
wrong: Analogue: two discrete values; digital: any in a range
Digital is wireless; analogue uses cables
Digital uses binary; analogue uses denary
cards.why: Digital input has two discrete values (1/0, ON/OFF, 5V/0V). Analogue input can have any value within a range and varies continuously.
cards.hook: Digital steps, analogue flows.

cards.q: You sketch voltage against time to show the difference between digital and analogue input. How is the digital input drawn?
cards.right: A square wave jumping between 0V and 5V
wrong: A smooth, continuously varying curve
A straight line sloping from 0V up to 5V
A flat line staying at 5V
cards.why: Digital has only two discrete values (5V = ON, 0V = OFF), so it jumps between two levels: a square wave. The smooth curve is the analogue signal.
cards.hook: Digital looks like steps (square), analogue like waves (smooth).

cards.q: In the context of embedded systems, what is meant by the term 'real-time'?
cards.right: It responds to inputs within a stated, short time
wrong: It shows the current time of day on a display
It processes inputs in batches at set times
It stays switched on 24 hours a day, every day
cards.why: Real-time systems respond to external stimuli within a stated (minimum) time, e.g. an alarm sounds immediately when a PIR sensor detects movement.
cards.hook: Real-time = no waiting: input in, response out, at once.
keys: respond to external stimuli within a stated

cards.q: Which of these is an example of a real-time embedded system?
cards.right: An alarm that sounds as soon as movement is sensed
wrong: A payroll program run at the end of each month
A laptop that backs up files every Friday
A spreadsheet that totals the day's sales
cards.why: A real-time system must react within a stated time: the alarm sounds immediately when a PIR sensor detects movement. The others can run later with no harm.
cards.hook: Ask: would a delay matter? Airbags and alarms: yes. Payroll: no.

cards.q: Which is an advantage of embedded systems over general purpose computers such as desktops and laptops?
cards.right: Cheaper and more reliable, as they do one job
wrong: They can run any program the user installs
They have more memory and storage
They are easier for users to reprogram
cards.why: Embedded systems are generally cheaper, often less complex and so more reliable, faster on a dedicated micro-controller, automated, portable and low power.
cards.hook: One job only: cheaper, smaller, simpler, more reliable.
keys: less complex and so more reliable

cards.q: A washing machine's embedded system runs its programme once started. Which advantage over a laptop does this show?
cards.right: Automated: minimal user intervention once started
wrong: Portability: it can easily be carried anywhere
General purpose: it can run any software at all
Upgradable: users can add more RAM and storage
cards.why: Embedded systems are automated: once started they need minimal user intervention. A laptop is general purpose and needs a user to run programs.
cards.hook: Press start and walk away: that's an embedded system.
keys: once started they need minimal user intervention

cards.q: An embedded system is hardware and software designed for one specific function, as part of a larger system. Which is an embedded system on a smartphone?
cards.right: The GPS receiver that finds the phone's location
wrong: A game the user downloads from an app store
The photos saved in the phone's storage
The phone number stored on the SIM card
cards.why: The camera, GPS, voice recognition, microphone or fingerprint reader each has its own hardware and software for one job. A downloaded app is just software; photos are data.
cards.hook: Embedded = a part with its own chip and code doing one job.
keys: its own hardware and software for one job

cards.q: Registers and RAM are both types of volatile memory. What is volatile memory?
cards.right: Holds data while on; all cleared when switched off
wrong: Keeps its contents even when the power is off
Can be read from but can never be written to
Memory held on secondary storage, such as a disk
cards.why: Volatile memory stores data and programs while the computer is on; it is called volatile because its entire contents are cleared when the computer is switched off.
cards.hook: Volatile = vanishes: power off, data gone.
keys: entire contents are cleared when the computer is switched off

cards.q: Which of these is NOT volatile memory?
cards.right: ROM
wrong: RAM
A CPU register
Cache memory
cards.why: Registers, cache and RAM all lose their contents when switched off. ROM (like SSDs and hard drives) is non-volatile: it keeps its data with no power.
cards.hook: Inside the CPU or in RAM: volatile. ROM and disks: kept.
keys: ROM (like SSDs and hard drives) is non-volatile

cards.q: Which of these correctly describes a difference between registers and RAM?
cards.right: Registers are inside the CPU and are much faster
wrong: RAM is inside the CPU and is much faster
Registers hold much more data than RAM does
Registers are cheaper per byte than RAM chips
cards.why: Registers are inside (part of) the CPU, so the CPU accesses them much faster than RAM. They cost more per byte, so they hold far less than RAM.
cards.hook: Registers: in the CPU's hand. RAM: on the desk beside it.
keys: Registers are inside (part of) the CPU

cards.q: Why does a CPU have only a handful of registers but gigabytes of RAM?
cards.right: Registers cost far more per byte than RAM
wrong: Registers are slower, so fewer are needed
Registers are non-volatile, so they last longer
RAM is inside the CPU, leaving no room
cards.why: Capacity follows cost: registers are much more expensive per byte than RAM, so a CPU holds only a few bytes in registers while RAM holds gigabytes.
cards.hook: Fastest memory = dearest memory = smallest amount.

cards.q: Moore's Law is about the number of transistors on an integrated circuit. What is a transistor?
cards.right: A semiconductor switch: on/off gives a 1 or 0
wrong: Many components on a single silicon chip
A wire carrying data between CPU and RAM
A memory cell that stores one byte
cards.why: A transistor is a type of electronic switch, a semiconductor device that switches signals; it is the building block of gates and is used to represent binary 1s and 0s.
cards.hook: Transistor = tiny switch; billions of them make a chip.

cards.q: What is an integrated circuit?
cards.right: Many components combined on a single silicon chip
wrong: A single switch that can represent a 1 or a 0
A board with separate chips joined by wires
The set of buses that join the CPU to the RAM
cards.why: An integrated circuit is a chip that contains multiple discrete components (mostly transistors) combined into logic circuits on a single silicon board. A CPU is one.
cards.hook: Integrated = all built in together on one chip.

cards.q: Moore's Law: the number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles about every two years. Why might it not remain accurate in the future?
cards.right: Physical limit to how many fit on one chip
wrong: Clock speeds cannot be pushed any higher
Chips will need more RAM than can be made
Binary numbers cannot count past 64 bits
cards.why: There is a physical limit to the number of transistors that can fit on a single chip: they are already a few nanometres wide, close to the size of atoms.
cards.hook: You can't shrink a switch smaller than the atoms it's made of.
keys: physical limit to the number of transistors

cards.q: A garage door opens on A AND (B OR C): A is the master switch, B and C are sensors. Rows ABC 000 and 001 give 0. What are the outputs for rows 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111?
cards.why: B OR C is 1 unless B = C = 0. With A = 0 the AND gives 0 (rows 010, 011); with A = 1 the output is just B OR C: 0 for 100, then 1, 1, 1.
cards.hook: Add a working column for the bracket, B OR C, first.

cards.q: In the 8-row truth table (A, B, C each 0 or 1) for the garage door statement A AND (B OR C), how many rows give an output of 1?
cards.why: The output is 1 only when A = 1 and at least one of B and C is 1: rows 101, 110 and 111, so 3 rows.
cards.hook: AND with A halves the table; OR then keeps 3 of the 4 rows.

cards.q: You draw the circuit diagram for the garage door, A AND (B OR C), using gate symbols. How are the gates connected?
cards.right: B, C into an OR; its output and A into an AND
wrong: A, B into an AND; its output and C into an OR
B, C into an AND; its output and A into an OR
A, B and C all into one 3-input AND gate
cards.why: The bracket is done first: B and C go into an OR gate giving B + C; that output and A go into an AND gate giving A.(B + C), which triggers the door.
cards.hook: Brackets first: the gate for the bracket sits nearest the inputs.
keys: B and C go into an OR gate

cards.q: Which symbol is drawn for the OR gate in the garage door circuit A AND (B OR C)?
cards.right: Curved back, pointed front
wrong: Flat back, round D-shaped front
Triangle with a small circle at the tip
Curved back with an extra curved line
cards.why: The OR gate has a curved back and a pointed front. The D shape with a flat back is AND, the triangle with a circle is NOT, and the extra curved line makes XOR.
cards.hook: AND is a D (for anD); OR is a pointed shield.
keys: curved back and a pointed front

cards.q: Figure 2 shows a Web Client, a Browser Request, a Web Server and a Server Response. In the client-server model, what happens first?
cards.right: The web client sends a browser request to the server
wrong: The web server sends a server response unasked
The web server sends a browser request to the client
Two web clients share files directly with each other
cards.why: A web client sends a browser request to a web server. The server processes the request and responds by sending the result back to the client as a server response.
cards.hook: Client asks, server answers: request out, response back.
keys: web client sends a browser request to a web server

cards.q: In the client-server model, what does the web server do with a browser request from a web client?
cards.right: Processes it and sends back a server response
wrong: Forwards it to the client's router to process
Stores it until the client sends a response
Displays the page on the server's own screen
cards.why: The web server processes the browser request (finding or building the page) and responds by sending the result back to the client as a server response.
cards.hook: The server serves: it does the work and sends the result back.

cards.q: Under the heading of cost, what is an advantage of cloud computing for a business?
cards.right: No up-front cost of buying servers
wrong: No fees: cloud storage is free to use
It costs less the longer you use it
The business owns the hardware it pays for
cards.why: There is no one-off up-front capital cost for hardware, and no upgrading or replacement costs: the cloud provider pays for those.
cards.hook: Cloud = renting, not buying: nothing big to pay at the start.

cards.q: Under the heading of cost, what is a disadvantage of cloud computing?
cards.right: Ongoing pay-as-you-go fees may cost more long-term
wrong: A large up-front bill for buying all the servers
The business must pay for hardware upgrades
Cloud data cannot be accessed when off-site
cards.why: Costs are ongoing (pay-as-you-go), which could work out more expensive in the long run than owning the hardware.
cards.hook: Rent never ends: small payments forever can beat one big one.

cards.q: Under the heading of impact on the environment, what is an advantage of cloud computing?
cards.right: Shared data centres use less energy per user
wrong: Cloud servers need no electricity at all to run
Data in the cloud takes up no physical space
Data centres need no cooling, unlike PCs
cards.why: Economies of scale let providers share services more efficiently, reducing the carbon footprint; many cloud companies generate their own energy, and less paper is used.
cards.hook: One big efficient kitchen beats a thousand small ones.

cards.q: Under the heading of impact on the environment, what is a disadvantage of cloud computing?
cards.right: More demand: more energy, bigger carbon footprint
wrong: It needs much more paper for keeping records
Every user must buy a more powerful new PC
Data centres share services and so save power
cards.why: Greater demand for cloud services increases the demand for energy (power and cooling for data centres), and so the carbon footprint.
cards.hook: The cloud is someone else's computer, and it still needs power.

cards.q: P(x, y) is in the top right quadrant if `x > 0 and y > 0`. Rows (x > 0, y > 0) are (F, F), (F, T), (T, F), (T, T); the first gives False. What do the last three rows give?
cards.right: False, False, True
wrong: True, True, True
True, True, False
True, False, True
cards.why: and is True only when both conditions are True. Rows (F, T) and (T, F) each contain one False, so False; (T, T) gives True: P is right of and above (0, 0).
cards.hook: One False sinks an and.
keys: True only when both conditions are True

cards.q: The test for the top right quadrant is `x > 0 and y > 0`. What does it give for the point (3, −2), and why?
cards.right: False, because y > 0 is False
wrong: True, because x > 0 is True
True, because 3 + (−2) > 0
False, because x > 0 is False
cards.why: x > 0 is True (3 > 0) but y > 0 is False (−2 < 0), so x > 0 and y > 0 is False: (3, −2) is in the bottom right quadrant.
cards.hook: and checks each condition separately; both must be True.

cards.q: A shaded square sits in the top left quadrant, with corners (−d, d) and (0, 0). Which Boolean expression is True for all points inside it?
cards.right: `(x > -d and x < 0) and (y > 0 and y < d)`
wrong: `(x > -d or x < 0) and (y > 0 or y < d)`
`(x > 0 and x < d) and (y > 0 and y < d)`
`(x > -d and x < 0) and (y > -d and y < 0)`
cards.why: The square runs from x = −d to x = 0 and from y = 0 to y = d, so −d < x < 0 and 0 < y < d; all four comparisons are joined with and.
cards.hook: Read the left, right, bottom and top edges, then and them all.

cards.q: For the square from x = −d to x = 0, why can the x-limits not be written `x > -d or x < 0`?
cards.right: It is True for every x, even x = 5d
wrong: It is False for every value of x
It is True only for x between −d and 0
It leaves out the point x = −d/2
cards.why: Any x is either greater than −d or less than 0 (or both), so the or is always True. A point must pass every test to be inside, so the tests are joined with and.
cards.hook: Between two limits = and. or lets everything through.

cards.q: User interfaces have become more user-friendly over 40 years. What is meant by the term 'user interface'?
cards.right: How the user gives input and the computer gives output
wrong: The software that controls the computer's hardware
The screen and keyboard, but not the software
The design rules that make a system accessible
cards.why: A user interface is the means by which the user provides input to a computer and the computer conveys output to the user: the point of interaction, through i/o devices.
cards.hook: Interface = the meeting point: commands in, feedback out.
keys: computer conveys output to the user

cards.q: Which type of user interface uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP), so the user clicks on images instead of typing?
cards.right: Graphical user interface (GUI)
wrong: Command line interface (CLI)
Menu-driven interface
Natural language interface
cards.why: A GUI uses windows, icons, menus and a pointing device (WIMP); the user interacts with images using a mouse, keyboard or touchscreen.
cards.hook: WIMP = Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer: that's a GUI.
keys: windows, icons, menus and a pointing device (WIMP)

cards.q: Which describes a command line interface (CLI)?
cards.right: Text only: the user types commands they must know
wrong: The user clicks on icons with a mouse pointer
The user picks from a list of options on screen
The user speaks commands aloud, as with Siri or Alexa
cards.why: A CLI is non-graphical and text-only: the user types commands, so must know them. Picking options is menu-driven; speech is a voice interface.
cards.hook: CLI: a blinking cursor waiting for you to type the right words.

cards.q: In the TCP/IP protocol suite, which layer breaks the message into small pieces called packets and numbers each one?
cards.right: Transport (host-to-host) layer
wrong: Application (process) layer
Network (internet) layer
Data link (network access) layer
cards.why: The transport layer breaks the message into packets; each gets a packet number and the total number of packets so the recipient can reassemble them in order.
cards.hook: Transport packs the message into numbered boxes.

cards.q: Which TCP/IP layer adds the sender's and the recipient's IP addresses, so the network knows where to send the message and where it came from?
cards.right: Network (internet) layer
wrong: Transport (host-to-host) layer
Application (process) layer
Data link (network access) layer
cards.why: The network layer adds the sender's and the recipient's IP addresses so the network knows where to send the message and where it came from.
cards.hook: Network layer writes the addresses on the envelope.
keys: adds the sender's and the recipient's IP addresses

cards.q: What happens within the application layer of TCP/IP?
cards.right: Message encoded with protocols like HTTP, FTP, SMTP
wrong: The message is split into numbered packets
The sender's and recipient's IP addresses are added
Packets are physically moved between nodes
cards.why: The application layer encodes/decodes the message into a form understood by sender and recipient, using protocols like HTTP, FTP and SMTP.
cards.hook: Application layer = the apps' own language: HTTP, FTP, SMTP.

cards.q: The transport layer gives each packet its packet number AND the total number of packets. Why include the total?
cards.right: So the recipient can tell if any packet is missing
wrong: So routers can choose the shortest path
So the recipient learns the sender's IP address
So the packets can be encrypted in order
cards.why: With each packet's number and the total, the recipient can reassemble the packets in order and see if any are missing (and ask for them again).
cards.hook: 'Page 3 of 7': you know at once if a page is missing.

cards.q: Smart homes use embedded systems to make living spaces more convenient. Which of these is an embedded system you might find in a smart home?
cards.right: A smart thermostat controlling the heating
wrong: A Raspberry Pi bought for learning to code
A laptop used to browse the Internet
A spreadsheet that tracks energy bills
cards.why: Heating control, lighting, alarms, smoke detectors, robots and smart appliances each do one job with their own chip. A Raspberry Pi or Micro:bit is not accepted.
cards.hook: Embedded = a computer hidden inside something that isn't 'a computer'.
keys: each do one job with their own chip

cards.q: Which characteristic distinguishes embedded systems from general computer systems?
cards.right: One specific function; can't be programmed beyond it
wrong: They can run any program that the user installs
They need a full keyboard, screen and mouse
They use much more power than a laptop or PC
cards.why: An embedded system performs a specific function and, unlike a general computer, cannot be programmed beyond what it was designed for; a PC can run any software.
cards.hook: Embedded: one job, for life. PC: any job you install.

cards.q: Compared with a general computer system, which of these is a characteristic of an embedded system?
cards.right: Minimal user interface; little human intervention
wrong: Large memory to hold many different programs
Frequent software changes to add new features
A general-purpose CPU able to run any app
cards.why: Embedded systems have a minimal user interface and need little human intervention; they are highly stable (rarely changed) and use microcontrollers with limited memory.
cards.hook: A few buttons, a tiny chip, and it gets on with the job.

cards.q: In the von Neumann architecture, data flows from input devices through the CPU and memory to output devices. What is meant by an output device?
cards.right: Hardware conveying information from computer to user
wrong: Hardware sending data from the user to the computer
Software that displays a program's results
Memory that keeps the results of processing
cards.why: An output device is any piece of hardware used to convey information from the computer to the user: a screen, printer, speaker or headphones.
cards.hook: Output goes OUT of the computer, to you.
keys: convey information from the computer to the user

cards.q: Which pair are both output devices?
cards.right: A monitor and a printer
wrong: A keyboard and a mouse
A monitor and a keyboard
A printer and a scanner
cards.why: A monitor (screen) and a printer both convey information from the computer to the user. A keyboard, mouse and scanner send data into the computer: input devices.
cards.hook: Can you see, hear or hold the result? Output. Do you put data in? Input.

cards.q: The CPU cycle that processes data and instructions has three steps. The first is 'Fetch Instruction'. What are the next two steps, in order?
cards.right: Decode, then Execute
wrong: Execute, then Decode
Decode, then Store
Process, then Output
cards.why: After fetching, the control unit decodes the instruction (works out what it means), then the CPU executes it. The right names in the wrong order earn 1 mark.
cards.hook: Fetch it, Decode it, Execute it: F-D-E, then round again.

cards.q: The CPU's registers include the Program Counter (PC) and the Accumulator (ACC). Which states a difference between them?
cards.right: PC: address of next instruction; ACC: data used
wrong: PC: data being used; ACC: address of next instruction
PC: the next instruction itself; ACC: its address
PC: results of the ALU; ACC: the next address
cards.why: The Program Counter contains the address of the next instruction to be executed, whereas the Accumulator stores data to be operated on (e.g. the ALU's result).
cards.hook: PC points the way (an address); ACC accumulates the answers (data).
keys: stores data to be operated on

cards.q: Where in the CPU are the Program Counter and the Accumulator typically found?
cards.right: PC in the Control Unit; ACC in the ALU
wrong: PC in the ALU; ACC in the Control Unit
Both in primary memory (RAM)
PC in RAM; ACC in the Control Unit
cards.why: The PC is typically part of the control unit, which fetches instructions, whereas the ACC is typically found in the ALU, which does the calculations.
cards.hook: The CU follows the program (PC); the ALU does the maths (ACC).
keys: PC is typically part of the control unit

cards.q: The CPU is made up of the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) and the Control Unit (CU). What is the purpose of the ALU?
cards.right: Performs arithmetic and logical operations
wrong: Directs and coordinates the CPU's operations
Holds the address of the next instruction
Stores the programs and data in use
cards.why: The ALU performs all the basic arithmetic operations (adding, subtracting) and logical operations (comparisons, AND, OR, NOT).
cards.hook: Arithmetic Logic Unit: the name says it: maths and logic.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the Control Unit (CU) in the CPU?
cards.right: Directs and coordinates the computer's operations
wrong: Performs the calculations and comparisons
Stores programs and data while the computer is on
Holds the result of the ALU's last calculation
cards.why: The CU directs and coordinates most of the operations in the computer, instructing the memory, ALU and input and output devices how to respond to the program's instructions.
cards.hook: The CU is the conductor: it plays nothing, it directs everyone.
keys: directs and coordinates most of the operations

cards.q: A program checks whether A is greater than B. Which part of the CPU carries out this comparison?
cards.right: The ALU, as a logical operation
wrong: The Control Unit, as it decides
The Program Counter
Primary memory (RAM)
cards.why: Comparisons are logical operations, done by the ALU along with arithmetic. The CU only directs: it decodes the instruction and signals the ALU to do it.
cards.hook: Compare or calculate: ALU. Coordinate: CU.

cards.q: Clock speed is one factor that impacts CPU performance. How does a higher clock speed make the CPU faster?
cards.right: More pulses per second: more fetch-decode-execute
wrong: More cores work on separate tasks at the same time
Each instruction carries more bits of data at once
Data the CPU needs next is kept close at hand
cards.why: Clock speed is the number of pulses per second (Hz); more pulses means more fetch-decode-execute cycles each second, so more instructions are processed.
cards.hook: Each tick of the clock drives the cycle round: faster ticks, more work.

cards.q: Why does a quad-core CPU usually perform better than a single-core CPU with the same clock speed?
cards.right: Each core fetches, decodes and executes its own
wrong: Each core runs at four times the clock speed
The cores share one fetch-decode-execute cycle
It comes with four times as much RAM
cards.why: Each core fetches, decodes and executes its own instructions, so more cores process more instructions in a given time, e.g. four tasks at once.
cards.hook: Four cooks in the kitchen, each with their own recipe.
keys: more cores process more instructions in a given time

cards.q: How does a bigger cache improve CPU performance?
cards.right: Less waiting: likely data is kept in fast memory
wrong: It adds secondary storage for virtual memory
It raises the clock pulses per second
It keeps the data when the power is off
cards.why: Cache is fast, small memory in the processor storing the instructions and data most likely to be needed, so the CPU waits less for slower RAM.
cards.hook: Cache = the CPU's pocket: what you use most, kept closest.
keys: fast, small memory in the processor

cards.q: Sarah will carry her new laptop around. You recommend a solid state drive over a magnetic hard drive. Which justification fits?
cards.right: No moving parts, so it copes with knocks
wrong: Data stored magnetically survives drops
Cheaper per gigabyte, so more capacity
Unlimited writes, unlike a magnetic drive
cards.why: An SSD has no moving parts, so it is more reliable and durable and better for transporting; it is also faster, quieter, smaller and uses less power.
cards.hook: Carried about? Nothing spinning means nothing to break.

cards.q: Sarah is choosing between magnetic and solid state drives. If you recommend the magnetic hard drive, which justification earns the marks?
cards.right: Cheaper per GB, so far more storage
wrong: Faster, as there are no moving parts
More durable if the laptop is dropped
Uses less power, so longer battery life
cards.why: Magnetic drives are cheaper per gigabyte and therefore give greater capacity; data can be overwritten directly (SSDs have a write limit), and it is a longer-proven technology.
cards.hook: HDD wins on price per GB; SSD wins on almost everything else.

cards.q: A computer carrying out lots of tasks can run out of memory and rely on virtual memory. What is meant by 'virtual memory'?
cards.right: Secondary storage used as extra RAM when RAM is full
wrong: Extra RAM chips built into the CPU to add space
Memory held in the cloud over the Internet
ROM used to hold data temporarily when RAM is full
cards.why: Virtual memory is an area of secondary storage (hard drive) allocated by the operating system to store data from RAM temporarily, usually when RAM is full.
cards.hook: Virtual = pretend RAM, borrowed from the disk.

cards.q: Why does a computer slow down when it relies heavily on virtual memory?
cards.right: Secondary storage is much slower than RAM
wrong: Virtual memory is volatile, so data is lost
The CPU must decode each instruction twice
Virtual memory is reached over the Internet
cards.why: Data in virtual memory takes longer to access and process as it is no longer in RAM: the drive is far slower, so the CPU waits.
cards.hook: Borrowed memory is slow memory.
keys: takes longer to access and process

cards.q: Sarah's group will work on a project both at school and at home. What is an advantage of working in the cloud?
cards.right: All can edit the latest files from anywhere
wrong: It works with no Internet connection
Files are kept only on the school's server
Each member keeps a separate copy offline
cards.why: Cloud files are available 24/7 from anywhere with internet, so every member can open and edit the latest version, even at the same time: it supports collaboration.
cards.hook: One copy in the cloud, everyone working on it.

cards.q: What is a disadvantage of Sarah's group working in the cloud?
cards.right: No Internet connection means no access to the work
wrong: Files can only be opened on the computer that made them
Files cannot be shared with other classmates
Work is lost whenever a laptop is switched off
cards.why: Cloud work needs internet connectivity: if the school Wi-Fi or someone's broadband is down, they cannot work. Vendor lock-in, costs and limited control are other drawbacks.
cards.hook: No connection, no cloud.

cards.q: Give the output (0 or 1) of each gate, in order: AND with 1, 1; AND with 0, 1; NOT with 1; OR with 1, 0; OR with 0, 0; NAND with 1, 1.
cards.why: AND needs every input 1: 1, then 0. NOT flips 1 to 0. OR needs at least one 1: 1, then 0. NAND is NOT(1 AND 1) = NOT 1 = 0.
cards.hook: AND: all 1s. OR: any 1. NOT: flip. NAND: AND, then flip.

cards.q: Column A shows the gates by their symbols. How do you tell the NAND gate's symbol from the AND gate's?
cards.right: NAND has a small circle on its output
wrong: NAND has a curved back and pointed front
NAND has an extra curved line at the back
NAND is drawn as a triangle
cards.why: Both are the D shape (flat back, round front); a small circle on the output adds a NOT, so the gate is NAND. The pointed shape is OR, the extra line XOR, the triangle NOT.
cards.hook: A bubble on the output means 'then flip it'.
keys: a small circle on the output adds a NOT

cards.q: RAM and ROM are two types of primary memory. Which is an example of data that might be stored in ROM?
cards.right: The BIOS (bootstrap program) run at start-up
wrong: A document being edited in a word processor
A Python program that is running now
Web pages open in the browser
cards.why: ROM holds permanent data the device needs: firmware, the BIOS essential for start-up, bootstrap programs, configuration. Documents and running programs are in RAM.
cards.hook: ROM = what the computer needs before anything else loads.

cards.q: Which is an example of data that might be stored in RAM?
cards.right: The document you are editing right now
wrong: The BIOS the computer needs at start-up
The firmware built into a device
The bootstrap program that loads the OS
cards.why: RAM holds temporary data in use: the operating system, open applications, running programs and documents being edited, all lost when the power goes off.
cards.hook: RAM = what you're working on now; ROM = what never changes.

cards.q: Two key functions of an operating system are resource management and file management. What is meant by resource management?
cards.right: Sharing out CPU time, RAM, storage and I/O devices
wrong: Keeping track of where each file is stored on disk
Saving backup copies of all files to the cloud
Installing the apps that the user has downloaded
cards.why: Resource management is how the OS controls and coordinates the computer's hardware resources such as CPU time, memory (RAM), secondary storage and input/output devices.
cards.hook: Resources = hardware. The OS decides who gets what, and when.
keys: controls and coordinates the computer's hardware resources

cards.q: What is meant by file management, as a function of an operating system?
cards.right: Organising files on storage so they can be used
wrong: Deciding how much CPU time each program gets
Giving each running program its share of RAM
Choosing which program may use the printer
cards.why: File management is how the OS organises and keeps track of files on storage devices (hard drives, USB drives) so they can be created, accessed or modified when needed.
cards.hook: File management = folders, names, where it's stored, who can open it.
keys: organises and keeps track of files on storage devices

cards.q: Two programs are running, and the OS gives each a turn on the CPU and its own part of RAM. Which function of the operating system is this?
cards.right: Resource management
wrong: File management
User interface
Device driver installation
cards.why: CPU time and RAM are hardware resources: controlling and sharing them out between running programs is resource management.
cards.hook: CPU time and RAM are resources; files are not.
keys: CPU time and RAM are hardware resources

cards.q: Distinguish between the IP and VoIP communication protocols.
cards.right: IP sends all data in packets; VoIP is IP for calls
wrong: VoIP sends all data in packets; IP is for calls
IP is for wired networks; VoIP for wireless ones
VoIP is IP with encryption added, like HTTPS
cards.why: IP is the general protocol for sending all types of data in packets over the internet (websites, emails); VoIP is a specific application of IP for voice and video.
cards.hook: IP carries everything; VoIP is IP carrying your voice.
keys: general protocol for sending all types of data

cards.q: Which of these is an example of VoIP being used?
cards.right: A WhatsApp or Zoom call
wrong: Browsing a website
Sending an email
Looking up a domain name
cards.why: VoIP is used for voice and video communication, e.g. Zoom and WhatsApp calls. Browsing and email use IP in general; looking up a name is DNS.
cards.hook: Talking over the internet? That's VoIP.

cards.q: What does VoIP stand for?
cards.right: Voice over Internet Protocol
wrong: Video over Internet Protocol
Voice over Intranet Packets
Virtual Online Internet Protocol
cards.why: VoIP is Voice over Internet Protocol: speech is digitised and sent as IP packets, so calls can be made over the internet.
cards.hook: Voice, riding over IP.

cards.q: Which CPU component generates a consistent timing signal that synchronises the CPU's operations and sets the speed at which it processes data?
cards.right: The clock
wrong: The Control Unit
The cache
The Program Counter
cards.why: The clock generates a consistent timing signal (clock pulse) that synchronises the CPU's operations and sets the processing speed, measured in GHz.
cards.hook: The clock is the CPU's drumbeat: every step happens on a tick.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the registers in the CPU?
cards.right: Small, fast stores for data, instructions, addresses
wrong: Large stores holding every program that is running
Permanent stores holding the start-up instructions
Units that carry out the arithmetic and logic
cards.why: Registers are small, high-speed storage locations within the CPU that temporarily hold data, instructions or addresses during processing (e.g. PC, MAR, MDR, accumulator).
cards.hook: Registers: tiny, fastest, inside the CPU, holding what's needed this instant.
keys: small, high-speed storage locations within the CPU

cards.q: Which CPU component stores frequently accessed data and instructions close to the CPU, to reduce latency and improve processing speed?
cards.right: Cache
wrong: RAM (main memory)
Virtual memory
The Program Counter
cards.why: Cache stores frequently accessed data and instructions close to the CPU to reduce latency. RAM is outside the CPU and slower; virtual memory is on secondary storage.
cards.hook: Cache keeps the favourites within arm's reach.
keys: frequently accessed data and instructions close to the CPU
